stem_md:
A  $\emph{tetromino tile}$  is a tile that can be formed by gluing together four unit square tiles, edge to edge. For each positive integer  $\emph{n}$ , consider a bathroom whose floor is in the shape of a  $2\times2 n$  rectangle. Let  $T_n$  be the number of ways to tile this bathroom floor with tetromino tiles. For example,  $T_2 = 4$  since there are four ways to tile a  $2\times4$  rectangular bathroom floor with tetromino tiles, as shown below.
[click for diagram]
Prove that each of the numbers  $T_1, T_2, T_3, ...$  is a perfect square.

**Attachments:**

![Screen Shot 2020-06-16 at 1.54.07 PM.png](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/d/9/1dae489d4d8bc96d1120fd38078989840c62ba.png)
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution, Hidden For Length</summary>**Lemma:** A bathroom floor tiling can never have the tetromino 
[asy]
size(2cm);
draw((0,0)--(2,0)--(2,1)--(3,1)--(3,2)--(1,2)--(1,1)--(0,1)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,1)--(2,1)--(2,2), dashed);

[/asy] 
*Proof:* 
[asy]
import olympiad;
import geometry;
pair a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j, k, l;
a = (0,0);
b = (10,0);
c = (10,2);
d = (0,2);
e = (3,0);
f = (5,0);
g = (6,2);
h = (4,2);
i = (5,1);
j = (6,1);
k = (4,1);
l = (3,1);

path t = e--f--i--j--g--h--k--l--cycle;
path left = a--e--l--k--h--d--cycle;
path right = b--c--g--j--i--f--cycle;


draw(a--b--c--d--cycle, linewidth(1.2));
filldraw(t, blue+white, linewidth(1.4));
filldraw(left, palered);
filldraw(right, palegreen);
draw((0,1)--(10,1), linewidth(0.3));
for (int z = 0; z<11; ++z) {
	draw((z,0)--(z,2),linewidth(0.3));
}
[/asy]
Consider the above diagram. The blue tetromino is being used to tile the bathroom floor, and it splits the floor into two sectors (in red and green). Both of these sectors have an odd number of tiles, so no number of tetrominoes can tile them completely. Thus, the bathroom floor cannot be covered with tiles if the blue tetromino is in use.  $\square$ Define a *break* in a tiling to be any vertical segment measuring two units formed by the edges of tiles, except at the border of the bathroom (this means not every tiling has a break). For example,
[asy]
import olympiad;
import geometry;
pair a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j;
a = (0,2);
b = (2,2);
c = (5,2);
d = (6,2);
e = (6,0);
f = (3,0);
g = (2,0);
h = (0,0);
i = (3,1);
j = (5,1);

path p = a--b--g--h--cycle;
path q = b--c--j--i--f--g--cycle;
path r = c--d--e--f--i--j--cycle;


draw(a--d--e--h--cycle, linewidth(1.2));
filldraw(p, palemagenta);
filldraw(q, paleblue);
filldraw(r, palegreen);

draw((0,1)--(6,1), linewidth(0.2));
for (int z = 0; z<7; ++z) {
	draw((z,0)--(z,2),linewidth(0.3));
}
draw(b--g, red+linewidth(1.2));
draw(ellipse((2,1), 0.2, 1.2), linewidth(0.5));


[/asy]
in the above diagram, the circled red segment is a break. We will now use casework on the location on the leftmost break in a tiling.

First, let  $a_n$  be the number of tilings of a  $2\times 2n$  floor with zero breaks. It is simple to see that  $a_1=1, a_2=3, \text{ and } a_3=2$ . We will show that  $n>3\implies a_n=2$ .

*Proof:* Consider the following diagram. 
[asy]
import olympiad;
import geometry;
size(4cm);
pair a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j;
a = (0,2);
b = (10,2);
c = (10,0);
d = (0,0);
e = (6,0);
f = (3,0);
g = (2,0);
h = (0,0);
i = (3,1);
j = (5,1);


draw(a--b--c--d--cycle, linewidth(1.2));
draw((0,1)--(10,1), linewidth(0.3));
for (int z = 0; z<11; ++z) {
	draw((z,0)--(z,2),linewidth(0.3));
}

[/asy]
[asy]
size(2cm);
draw((0,0)--(4,0)--(4,1)--(0,1)--cycle);
for (int i = 1; i<4; ++i) {
	draw((i,1)--(i,0),linewidth(0.5));
}
label(" $A=$ ", (-1.7,0.5));

[/asy]
[asy]
size(2cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,2)--(2,2)--(2,1)--(0,1)--cycle);
for (int i = 1; i<3; ++i) {
	draw((i,1)--(i,0),linewidth(0.5));
}
draw((2,1)--(3,1),linewidth(0.5));
label(" $B=$ ", (-1.7,0.5));

[/asy]
Clearly, a tiling with no breaks cannot have a  $2\times 2$  tetromino, so it is comprised of only  $A$  and  $B$  pieces. Consider the top left tile of the floor. If we place an  $A$  tile there, then we must also have an  $A$  tile directly beneath it, and this forms a break  $4$  units into the floor. If we place a  $B$  tile's longer end there, then the short end of the  $B$  tile forms a break  $3$  units in. Therefore, we must place a  $B$  tile so that it covers up the leftmost edge, and two extra tiles protrude to the right. There are to ways to do this, and they are reflections of each other. Then, we are left with the following (or its reflection):
[asy]
import olympiad;
import geometry;
size(4cm);
pair a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j;
a = (0,2);
b = (10,2);
c = (10,0);
d = (0,0);
e = (1,2);
f = (1,1);
g = (3,1);
h = (3,0);
i = (3,1);
j = (5,1);

filldraw(a--e--f--g--h--d--cycle, paleblue,invisible);
draw(a--b--c--d--cycle, linewidth(1.2));
draw((0,1)--(10,1), linewidth(0.3));
for (int z = 0; z<11; ++z) {
	draw((z,0)--(z,2),linewidth(0.3));
}

[/asy]
We must cover the empty part of the upper row without creating a break, so we cannot tile it like so:
[asy]
import olympiad;
import geometry;
size(4cm);
pair a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j;
a = (0,2);
b = (10,2);
c = (10,0);
d = (0,0);
e = (1,2);
f = (1,1);
g = (3,1);
h = (3,0);
i = (3,1);
j = (5,1);

filldraw(a--e--f--g--h--d--cycle, paleblue,invisible);
filldraw(e--(4,2)--(4,0)--h--g--f--cycle, palered, invisible);
draw(a--b--c--d--cycle, linewidth(1.2));
draw((0,1)--(10,1), linewidth(0.3));
for (int z = 0; z<11; ++z) {
	draw((z,0)--(z,2),linewidth(0.3));
}

[/asy]
The only other way to tile this is like so:
[asy]
import olympiad;
import geometry;
size(4cm);
pair a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j;
a = (0,2);
b = (10,2);
c = (10,0);
d = (0,0);
e = (1,2);
f = (1,1);
g = (3,1);
h = (3,0);
i = (3,1);
j = (5,1);

filldraw(a--e--f--g--h--d--cycle, paleblue,invisible);
filldraw(e--(5,2)--(5,1)--f--cycle, palered, invisible);
draw(a--b--c--d--cycle, linewidth(1.2));
draw((0,1)--(10,1), linewidth(0.3));
for (int z = 0; z<11; ++z) {
	draw((z,0)--(z,2),linewidth(0.3));
}

[/asy]
Continuing in this fashion, we must keep using  $A$  tiles until we reach the rightmost edge, and our tiling looks like this (or its reflection):
[asy]
import olympiad;
import geometry;
size(4cm);
pair a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j;
a = (0,2);
b = (10,2);
c = (10,0);
d = (0,0);
e = (1,2);
f = (1,1);
g = (3,1);
h = (3,0);
i = (3,1);
j = (5,1);

filldraw(a--e--f--g--h--d--cycle, paleblue);
filldraw(e--(5,2)--(5,1)--f--cycle, palered);
filldraw(g--(7,1)--(7,0)--h--cycle, palered);
filldraw((5,2)--(9,2)--(9,1)--(5,1)--cycle, palered);
filldraw(b--c--(7,0)--(7,1)--(9,1)--(9,2)--cycle, paleblue);
draw(a--b--c--d--cycle, linewidth(1.2));
draw((0,1)--(10,1), linewidth(0.3));
for (int z = 0; z<11; ++z) {
	draw((z,0)--(z,2),linewidth(0.3));
}

[/asy]
Since the only two tilings of this floor without a break are this and its reflection,  $a_n=2$ .  $\square$ Now, we are ready for our casework. Let  $p$  be the *position* of the first (if any) break in a tiling, where a position  $k$  is the segment of length  $2$  parallel to the leftmost edge of the floor and  $k$  units away from the leftmost edge of the floor. It is easy to see that  $$ n\ge 3\implies T_n=\left(\sum_{i = 1}^{n-1}a_{i}T_{n-i}\right)+2=T_{n-1}+3T_{n-2}+2T_{n-3}+2T_{n-4}+2T_{n-5}+\cdots+2T_{1}+2, $$  by letting  $i$  be the position of the first break in the tiling (the last  $2$  in the sum accounts for the two tilings with zero breaks). It is easy to verify that  $T_1=1, T_2=4, T_3=9,T_4=25$  and this identity holds for those values. Now, for  $n\ge 4$ , note that  $$ T_n=T_{n-1}+3T_{n-2}+2T_{n-3}+2T_{n-4}+2T_{n-5}+\cdots+2T_{1}+2 $$    $$ \implies T_n=T_{n-1}+\left(2T_{n-2}-T_{n-3}\right)+\left(T_{n-2}+3T_{n-3}+2T_{n-4}+2T_{n-5}+\cdots+2T_{1}+1\right) $$    $$ \implies T_n=2T_{n-1}+2T_{n-2}-T_{n-3}. $$  Now, we have that  $T_1=1, T_2=4, T_3=9$ , and  $T_n=2T_{n-1}+2T_{n-2}-T_{n-3}$ . I claim that  $T_n=F_{n+1}^2$  satisfies this recurrence, where  $F_k$  is the Fibonacci sequence and  $F_0=0,F_1=1$ ; this also holds for  $n=1, 2, 3, 4$ . By Cassini's Identity,  $F_k^2=F_{k+1}F_{k-1}+(-1)^{k-1}$ , so  $$ F_{n+1}^2=2F_n^2+2F_{n-1}^2-F_{n-2}^2 $$    $$ \iff F_{n+2}F_n +(-1)^n=2\left(F_{n+1}F_{n-1}+(-1)^{n-1}+F_nF_{n-2}+(-1)^{n-2} \right)-F_{n-1}F_{n-3}-(-1)^{n-3} $$    $$ \iff F_{n+2}F_n = 2\left(F_{n+1}F_{n-1}+F_nF_{n-2}\right)-F_{n-1}F_{n-3} $$    $$ \iff F_{n+1}F_{n-2}+F_nF_{n-1}=F_{n+1}F_{n-1}+F_nF_{n-2}-F_{n-1}F_{n-3} $$    $$ \iff (F_{n+1}-F_n)(F_{n-2}-F_{n-1})=-F_{n-1}F_{n-3}, $$  which is true since  $F_{k}=F_{k-1}+F_{k-2}$ . All of our steps are reversible, so  $T_n=F_{n+1}^2$  satisfies the recurrence, and thus all  $T_n$  are perfect squares.</details>

stem_md:
Let  $ABCD$  be a square. For a point  $P$  inside  $ABCD$ , a  $\emph{windmill}$  centred at  $P$  consists of two perpendicular lines  $l_1$  and  $l_2$  passing through  $P$ , such that $\quad\bullet$   $l_1$  intersects the sides  $AB$  and  $CD$  at  $W$  and  $Y$ , respectively, and $\quad\bullet$   $l_2$  intersects the sides  $BC$  and  $DA$  at  $X$  and  $Z$ , respectively.
A windmill is called  $\emph{round}$  if the quadrilateral  $WXYZ$  is cyclic. 
Determine all points  $P$  inside  $ABCD$  such that every windmill centred at  $P$  is round.

**Attachments:**

![Screen Shot 2020-06-16 at 1.54.12 PM.png](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/5/0/e575ad6e97c69f31015dc09f059523456f852b.png)
solution_md: Suppose  $WXYZ$  is cyclic. Then since  $AWPZ$  is cyclic, we have  $\angle ZWP = \angle DAP$ . Using 3 other similar relations, we have  $\angle APD + \angle BPC = 180^\circ$  as an equivalent condition for each windmill centered at  $P$  being round. Consider the point  $R, S$  where  $(APD)$  meets  $AC, BD$ . Then we have (by symmetry across  $AC$ ), that  $\angle BRC = \angle DRC = 180^\circ - \angle ARD = 180^\circ - \angle APD = \angle BPC$ , so  $R$  is also on  $(BPC)$ , and analogously,  $S$  is on both  $(APD)$  and  $(BPC)$ . This implies that  $P = R$  or  $P = S$ . By reversing this argument, we can see that for any point  $P$  on the two diagonals, the problem condition is satisfied.

stem_md:
Let  $x,y,z$  be positive real numbers such that $x^4+y^4+z^4=1$  .
 Determine with proof the minimum value of
  $\frac{x^3}{1-x^8}+\frac{y^3}{1-y^8}+\frac{z^3}{1-z^8}$
solution_md:
Here's the TLT solution. It's cleaner than it looks, actually.

The answer is  $\boxed{\frac{27\sqrt[4]3}8}$ . Let  $a = x^4, b = y^4, c = z^4$ . I claim that   $$ \sum \frac{a^{3/4}}{1-a^2} \geq \sum \frac {9 \sqrt[4] 3 a}8 = \frac{27\sqrt[4]3}8, $$   with equality holding when  $a=b=c=\frac 13$ . Indeed, it suffices to verify the inequality   $$ \frac{x^3}{1-x^8} \geq \frac{9\sqrt[4]3}8 x^4 \iff x(1-x^8) \leq \frac 8{9\sqrt[4]3}. $$   However, by AM-GM, we have   $$ \frac{8x^8+8(1-x^8)}9 \geq \sqrt[9]{(8x^8)(1-x^8)^8} \iff x^8(1-x^8)^8 \leq \frac{8^8}{9^9}, $$   which proves the result.

How did you use Tangent Line method? Did you let $f(x) = \frac{\sqrt[4]{x^3}}{1-x^2}$ and then find the tangent to it at $x=\frac{1}{3}$ ? Is it true in general that if we find tangent for $g(x^r)$ as $h(x)$ then $h(\sqrt[r]{x})$ is tangent to $g(x)$ ? After substituting different power of the input variable ( $x$ ) in a function what properties remain same and what changes?

The expressions are one variable functions, we can  use calculus to solve the problem, especially TLT. 
Firstyly, let  $a=x^4,b=y^4,c=z^4$    in order to  use TLT "better". Then  Let  $f(a)= \frac{a^{3/4}}{1-a^2}$ . We wish to minimize  $f(a)+f(b)+f(c)$  in subject to  $a+b+c=1$ . 

 One may calculate  $f'(a)=\frac{5a^2+3}{4a^{1/4}(1-a^2)^2}$ . By TLT, there are some value  $k$  such that
   $$  f(a) \ge f(k)+ f'(k)(a-k) $$    One of the obvious values is  $k=1/3$  which gives
     $$  f(a) \ge \frac{3^{5/4}}{8} +    \frac{9(3^{1/4})}{8}(a-\frac{1}{3}) $$      Then   $$ f(a)+f(b)+f(c) \ge \frac{27 \sqrt[4]{3}}{8} $$      It is suffient to show that  $\frac{x^3}{1-x^8} \ge \frac{9 \sqrt[4]{3}}{8}x^4 \Leftrightarrow 8 + x^9 3^{9/4} - 3^{9/4}x \ge 0$ . Which is straight by calculus since derivative of LHS is  $ 9\sqrt[4]{3}(9x^8-1)$  , which is  $0$  when  $x= \frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{3}}$ . Hence we are done.

[url = https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=factor+x*%281-x%5E8%29+-+8%2F%289*3%5E%281%2F4%29%29] Wolfram Alpha here[/url] (see "factorization over splitting field") shows that if one looks for constants  $A$  and  $B$  such that  $\frac{t^3}{1-t^8} \geq At^4 + B$  (with  $t = 3^{-1/4}$  being a double root), one would get  $B = 0$  and  $A = \frac{9\sqrt[4]{3}}{8}$  and that the remaining multiplier after factoring has all its coefficients positive, hence it is positive itself. Thus in principle the linearization trick can be done by hand even without derivatives, but would require a bit of annoying pain.

stem_md: Define a sequence  ${{a_n}}_{n\ge1}$  such that  $a_1=1$  ,  $a_2=2$  and  $a_{n+1}$  is the smallest positive integer  $m$  such that  $m$  hasn't yet occurred in the sequence and also  $gcd(m,a_n)\neq{1}$ . Show that all positive integers occur in the sequence.
solution_md: I claim at at some moment, some variable $a_i$ is divisible by prime $p$ , and this is possible infinitely many times. Observe that this solves the problem, hence it is enough to prove our claim.** Claim 1.** Any prime $p$ can divide by at least one integer $a_i$ . This is actually pretty logical, FTSOC, assume that there is some $p$ that none of the integers in sequence are divided by. Then smallest integer that is divisible by $p$ is $p$ itself. If at some point we have arbitrarly bigger $a_j= p_1^{b_1} \cdot p_2^{b_2} \cdot ... \cdot p_k^{b_3}$ , such that $pClaim 2.** Any prime $p$ can divide by infinitely many integers $a_i....a_j$ . FTSOC, assume otherwise. Let $p$ be a prime such that it can divide finitely many integers in our sequence. Let the biggest such integer be $a_i$ and let $a_i= p \cdot p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdot ... \cdot p_k$ . After arbitrarly bigger time, we will have arbitrarly bigger variable $a_j= q_1 \cdot q_2 \cdot ... \cdot q_m$ then our next smallest integer would be $p \cdot \prod q_i$ where $\prod q_i$ is product of some chosen primes from $a_j$ , hence contradiction. $\square$ . Note that the product will the minimum possible since by Claim 1. These claims and size reasons are enough to show that any primes occur in the sequence and indeed any product of primes occur in the sequence, hence we are done**Remark**: IMO this question is very logical and hence my solution is not very rigorous but it has the same ideas as the other solutions so I guess my solution is ok.

candidates:
Here is a more combinatorial way that I'd like to think this problem in.

Imagine we have a bucket for each prime  $p$ , and in the bucket for  $p$ , we have all multiples of  $p$  arranged increasingly from the top to the bottom. 

Each time when we want to compute the next term, we do the following. We look at which buckets the last term belongs to, remove the last term from all those buckets, and the next term is the smallest number among the numbers at the top of those buckets. We repeatedly do this procedure.

With this in mind, we can prove the following.

Lemma 1. It suffices to show that any number in the bucket for  $2$  appears in the sequence.
<details><summary>Proof</summary>If any number in the bucket for  $2$  appears, then for any  $m\in\mathbb{N}$ , we know that we can find  $i_1<i_2<\ldots<i_m$  such that  $m|a_{i_j}$  for all  $1\leq j\leq m$ . If none of  $a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_m}$  is equal to  $m$ , then by definition, they are all smaller than  $m$ . This is a contradiction to the assumption that they are distinct.</details>

Lemma 2. If some number in the bucket for  $2$  does not appear, then only finitely many even numbers appear.
<details><summary>Proof</summary>The proof proceeds similarly as Lemma 1. If infinitely many even numbers appear, then for any even number  $2k$  we can find  $i_1<\ldots<i_{2k}$  such that  $2|a_{i_j}$  for all  $1\leq j\leq 2k$ . Then with the same argument we can deduce that there exists  $1\leq j\leq 2k$  such that  $a_{i_j}=2k$ . This is a contradiction with the assumption.</details>

Lemma 3. If there are only finitely many even numbers, then  $a_n<a_{n+1}$  for finitely many positive integers.
<details><summary>Proof</summary>Let  $N$  be a positive integer so that  $a_{N+1},a_{N+2},\ldots$  are all odd. For each  $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , let  $p(n)$  be the label for the bucket we take  $a_{n+1}$  from (note that there might be a tie among the buckets, in which case we choose the bucket with the smallest label). Then we know that  $p(n)\geq 3$  for all  $n\geq N$ . Now if  $n> N$  satisfies that  $a_n<a_{n+1}$ , then we know that  $a_{n+1}=p(n)(a_n/p(n)+k)$  for some positive integer  $k$ . Since both  $a_n$  and  $a_{n+1}$  are odd, we know that  $k\geq 2$ . This shows that there is some  $i\leq N$  such that  $a_i=p(n)(a_n/p(n)+1)=a_n+p(n)$ . Therefore, if  $S$  is the set of  $n>N$  with  $a_n<a_{n+1}$ , then we can construct a well-defined map  $f:S\to [N]$  so that  $a_{f(n)}=a_n+p(n)$ .

For each  $i\in [N]$ , we know that if  $f(n)=i$  then  $a_i=a_n+p(n)$ . This shows that  $p(n)|a_i$ , and so that if  $a_i$  has  $k$  different prime factors, then there are at most  $k$  elements in  $S$  that are sent to  $i$  by  $f$ . In particular, any element in  $[N]$  is hit by  $f$  only finitely many times, which shows that  $S$  is a finite set.</details>

Now by Lemma 2. and Lemma 3., we know that if some multiple of  $2$  does not appear, then the sequence  $a_1,a_2,\ldots$  can only go up for finitely many times. This is a contradiction with that it is an infinite sequence of positive integers. Therefore all multiples of  $2$  appear, and by Lemma 1., we are done.

stem_md:
Consider an odd prime number  $p$  and  $p$  consecutive positive integers  $m_1,m_2,…,m_p$ .
Choose a permutation  $\sigma$  of  $1,2,…,p$  . 
Show that there exist two different numbers  $k,l\in{(1,2,…,p)}$  such that  $p\mid{m_k.m_{\sigma(k)}-m_l.m_{\sigma(l)}}$
solution_md:
This one's nice. 

First, WLOG  $m_{i} = i$  for  $i=1,...,p$ .

Now, assume for the sake of contradiction that this condition isn't satisfied for any pair  $(i,j)$ . This implies that  $k\sigma{(k)}$  covers the entire residue class  $\mod{p}$ . Now, this implies that  $\sigma{(p)}=p$ . 

Now, we have  $((p-1)!)^2=\prod_{n=1}^{p-1} n\sigma{(n)} \equiv (p-1)! \pmod{p}$ , which is clearly a contradiction by Wilson's theorem.  $\square$

stem_md: Find all functions  $u:R\rightarrow{R}$  for which there exists a strictly monotonic function  $f:R\rightarrow{R}$  such that  $f(x+y)=f(x)u(y)+f(y)$ for all  $x,y\in{\mathbb{R}}$
solution_md:
Find all functions $u:R\rightarrow{R}$ for which there exists a strictly monotonic function $f:R\rightarrow{R}$ such that $f(x+y)=f(x)u(y)+f(y)$ for all $x,y\in{\mathbb{R}}$
Let $P(x,y)$ be the assertion $f(x+y)=f(x)u(y)+f(y)$ $P(0,x)$ $\implies$ $f(0)u(x)=0$ and so $f(0)=0$ (else we get $f(x+y)=f(y)$ and so $f(x)$ is not strictly monotonic. $P(x,0)$ $\implies$ $f(x)(u(0)-1)=0$ and so $u(0)=1$ (else $f(x)$ is not strictly monotonic If $u(t)=0$ for some $t$ , then $P(x,t)$ implies $f(x+t)=f(t)$ , impossible since $f(x)$ strictly monotonic. So $u(x)\ne 0$ $\forall x$ Subtracting $P(x,y)$ from $P(y,x)$ , we get New assertion $Q(x,y)$ : $f(x)(u(y)-1)=f(y)(u(x)-1)$ If $u(t)=1$ for some $t\ne 0$ (so that $f(t)\ne 0$ ), then $Q(x,t)$ $\implies$ $u(x)=1$ $\forall x$ which indeed is a solution (choose $f(x)\equiv x$ for example). If $u(x)=1$ $\iff$ $x=0$ : $Q(x,1)$ $\implies$ $f(x)=c(u(x)-1)$ for some $c=\frac{f(1)}{u(1)-1}\ne 0$ Plugging this in original equation, we get $u(x+y)=u(x)u(y)$ Since we previously got $u(x)\ne 0$ $\forall x$ , this easily implies $u(x)>0$ $\forall x$ (set $x=y$ And so $\ln u(x)$ is additive. So $u(x)=e^{g(x)}$ where $g(x)$ is some additive function. If $g(x)$ is not linear, graph of $g(x)$ is dense in $\mathbb R^2$ and so graph of $f(x)$ is dense in $\mathbb R\times (-c,+\infty)$ (or $(-\infty,-c)$ if $c<0$ , in contradiction with $f(x)$ stricly monotonic. So $g(x)$ is linear and we got $\boxed{u(x)=e^{ax}\forall x}$ which indeed is a solution, whatever is $a\in\mathbb R$ , choosing for example $f(x)=e^{ax}-1$ if $a\ne 0$ or $f(x)=x$ if $a=0$

<details><summary>Solution</summary>We claim that the answer is all functions  $u(x) \equiv a^x$  for some  $a > 0.$ First let's demonstrate that these work. For  $u \equiv 1$ , simply take  $f \equiv x$ .

For  $u \equiv a^x$  for  $a > 1$ , take  $f(x) \equiv a^x - 1.$  This works as  $a^{x+y} - 1 = (a^x - 1) a^y + a^y -1.$ For  $u \equiv a^x$  for  $a < 1$ , take  $f(x) \equiv -(a^x - 1).$  This works analogously as the previous construction. 

Let's now show that these are the only such functions which work. 

Let  $P(x, y)$  be the assertion of the problem. We have from  $P(0, 0)$  that  $f(0) u(0) = 0$ . From  $P(x, 0)$  we get  $f(x) = f(x)u(0) + f(0),$  i.e.  $f(x) (1 - u(0))$  is constant. As  $f$  is nonconstant, this implies  $u(0) = 1$ , and  $f(0) u(0) = 0$  gives  $f(0) = 0.$  As a result of  $f$ 's monotonicity,  $f$  is nonzero for nonzero inputs. We hence have for all  $x \neq 0$  that:  $$ u(y) = \frac{f(x+y) - f(y)}{f(x)}. $$  Let  $Q(x, y)$  be the above assertion, for  $x \neq 0, y \in \mathbb{R}.$  We have from  $Q(x, y) + Q(x+y, y)$  that for all  $x \neq 0, -y$ :  $$ u(x+y) + u(y) = \frac{f(2x+y) - f(y)}{f(x)}. \qquad (1) $$  We have by  $Q(x, x)$  that:  $$ \frac{f(2x)}{f(x)} = u(x) + 1, $$  so using this we can turn  $(1)$  into:  $$ u(x+y) + u(y) = u(y) (u(x) + 1), $$  or  $$ u(x+y) = u(x) u(y), \forall x \in \mathbb{R} / \{0, -y\}. $$  From  $Q(-y, y) \cdot Q(y, -y)$  we get that the above actually holds when  $x = -y$  as well.

Since it clearly holds for  $x = 0$  ( $u(0) = 1$ ), we get:  $$ u(x+y) = u(x)u(y), \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}. \qquad (2) $$  We claim that this implies that  $u$  is exponential, i.e. there is some  $t$  such that  $u(x) = t^x.$ By taking advantage of pseudo-symmetry, we get from  $P(x, y) - P(y, x)$  that  $f(x)(u(y) - 1) = f(y)(u(x) - 1),$  so  $y = 1$  gives us  $f(x) (u(1) - 1) = f(1) (u(x) - 1).$  If  $u(1) = 1$ , then since  $f(1) > f(0) = 0$  we get  $u \equiv 1,$  which works.

Else,  $u$  is obtained from  $f$  by a suitable transformation (translation + dilation), which implies that  $u$  must also be either monotonically increasing or decreasing. In either case, it's clear that  $u$  must be exponential.</details>

stem_md: Let  $F$  be the set of all  $n-tuples$   $(A_1,A_2,…,A_n)$  such that each  $A_i$  is a subset of  ${1,2,…,2019}$ . Let  $\mid{A}\mid$  denote the number of elements o the set  $A$  . Find  $\sum_{(A_1,…,A_n)\in{F}}^{}\mid{A_1\cup{A_2}\cup...\cup{A_n}}\mid$
solution_md: Note that  $|F| = 2^{2019n}.$  We claim that the answer is  $2019(2^{2019n} - 2^{2018n}).$ Notice that we can rewrite the summation as:  $$ \sum_{e \in [2019]} \sum_{(A_1, A_2, \cdots, A_n) \in F | e \in A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \cdots \cup A_n} 1. $$  Indeed, notice that for a given  $e \in [2019]$ , there are  $2^{2018n}$    $n-$ tuples in  $F$  s.t.  $e \notin A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \cdots \cup A_n$  (simply  $2^{2018}$  ways to pick each  $A_i$  to not contain  $e$ ). This means that the inner sum is always  $2^{2019n} - 2^{2018n}$ , and so our answer is:  $$ \boxed{2019(2^{2019n} - 2^{2018n})}. $$   $\square$

stem_md:
$a,b,c$  are positive integer.
Solve the equation: $ 2^{a!}+2^{b!}=c^3 $
solution_md:
The only solution is  $\boxed{(2,2,2)}$ , which works. Now we show it's the only one. 

Claim: If the sum of two powers of  $2$  is a cube, then neither of the two powers of  $2$  are  $1 \pmod 7$ . 
Proof: Suppose otherwise  $2^x + 2^y = z^3$  for some nonnegative integers  $x,y,z$  and that one of  $2^x, 2^y$  are  $1 \pmod 7$ . WLOG that  $2^y \equiv 1 \pmod 7$ . Note that powers of  $2$  are  $1,2,$  or  $4$  modulo  $7$ , so  $z^3$  is  $2,3,$  or  $5$  modulo  $7$ , however cubes are either  $-1,0,1$  modulo  $7$ , absurd.  $\square$ Thus,  $6$  can't divide  $a!$  or  $b!$ , meaning  $a,b$  are both less than  $3$ . Checking cases ( $a=1,2$  and  $b=1,2$ ) gives the desired result.

Proof: Assume otherwise WLOG  $a < b$ , and let  $\frac{b!}{a!} = k$ .

solution_md: $\spadesuit \ \color{blue}{\textbf{Solution:}}$  By homogenizing the inequality, it's equivalent to proving that \[\sum_{cyc} \frac{a^2+\frac{2}{3}(a+b+c)^2}{2(a^2+b^2+c^2)+\frac{2a(a+b+c)}{3}-\frac{(a+b+c)^2}{3}}\le 3.\] we now show that  \[\frac{a^2+\frac{2}{3}(a+b+c)^2}{2(a^2+b^2+c^2)+\frac{2a(a+b+c)}{3}-\frac{(a+b+c)^2}{3}} \le 1.\] Simplifying the expressions, we will end up proving \[8a^2+11b^2+11c^2\ge 8ab+14bc+8ac\] which follows from AM-GM, \[4a^2+4b^2\ge 8ab\]\[4a^2+4c^2\ge 8ac\] \[7b^2+7c^2 \ge 14bc.\] The other 2 cases are similar, so \[\sum_{cyc} \frac{a^2+\frac{2}{3}(a+b+c)^2}{2(a^2+b^2+c^2)+\frac{2a(a+b+c)}{3}-\frac{(a+b+c)^2}{3}}\le \sum_{cyc} 1 = 3. \quad \blacksquare\]

$a,b,c$ are positive numbers. $a+b+c=3$ Prove that: $\sum \frac{a^2+6}{2a^2+2b^2+2c^2+2a-1}\leq 3 $
Applying **Cauchy-Schwarz inequality**, we have $$ 2b^2+2c^2 \enspace = \enspace (1+1) (b^2+c^2) \enspace \geq (b+c)^2 $$ and using the condition $a+b+c =3$ , this is equivalent to $$ \iff \quad 2b^2+2c^2 \enspace \geq \enspace (3-a)^2 \enspace = \enspace a^2-6a+9 $$ Adding $(2a^2+2a-1)$ to both sides, this is equivalent to $$ \iff \quad 2a^2+2b^2+2c^2+2a-1 \enspace \geq \enspace 3a^2 -8a +8 $$ $$ \iff \quad \frac{a^2+6}{3a^2-8a+8} \enspace \geq \enspace \frac{a^2+6}{2a^2+2b^2+2c^2+2a-1} \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad (1) $$ Now observe that the inequality $$ 1 \enspace \geq \enspace \frac{a^2+6}{3a^2-8a+8} \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad (2) $$ is equivalent to $$ \iff \quad 3a^2-8a+8 \enspace \geq \enspace a^2+6 $$ $$ \iff \quad 2(a-1)^2 \enspace \geq \enspace 0 $$ which is *obviously* true. Combining $(1)$ and $(2)$ , we obtain $$ 1 \enspace \geq \enspace \frac{a^2+6}{2a^2+2b^2+2c^2+2a-1} \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad (3) $$ Similarly we obtain $$ 1 \enspace \geq \enspace \frac{b^2+6}{2a^2+2b^2+2c^2+2b-1} \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad (4) $$ and $$ 1 \enspace \geq \enspace \frac{c^2+6}{2a^2+2b^2+2c^2+2c-1} \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad (5) $$ Adding the inequalities $(3)$ , $(4)$ and $(5)$ we get the desired inequality $$ 3 \enspace\geq \enspace\frac{a^2+6}{2a^2+2b^2+2c^2+2a-1} \enspace +\enspace \frac{b^2+6}{2a^2+2b^2+2c^2+2b-1} \enspace+\enspace\frac{c^2+6}{2a^2+2b^2+2c^2+2c-1} $$

Solve:  $a!+5^b=7^c$ *Proposed by Serbia*
solution_md: $Case$    $I:$   $b=0$ : Then  $a!+1=7^{c}$  and as  $7|a!$  when  $a\geq 7$ (in that case  $a!+1>0$ , so  $c>0$ ), then  $a\leq 6$ . A quick check gives the solution  $(a,b,c)=(3,0,1)$ . $Case$   $II:$   $b>0$ . Then  $a!+5^{b}>5^{b}>5$ , so  $c>0$ . If  $a>4$ , then  $5$  divides the LHS, but not the RHS, contradiction. Also, as  $5^{b}\equiv 7^{c}\equiv 1$  (mod  $2$ ), then  $2$  divides  $a!$ , so  $2\leq a\leq 4$ . $Case$   $2.1$ )   $a=2$ :  $2+5^{b}=7^{c}$ . If  $b=1$  we reach the solution  $(a,b,c)=(2,1,1)$ . If  $b>1$  modulo  $25$  yields  $7^{c}\equiv 2$  (mod  $25$ ), which is a contradiction as  $7^{c}\equiv 1,7,24,18$  (mod  $25$ ). $Case$   $2.2$ )   $a=3$ :  $6+5^{b}=7^{c}$ . Modulo  $3$  gives that  $b$  is even. Now looking modulo  $25$ ,  $LHS$  has residue  $6$  and  $7^{c}\equiv 1,7,24,18$  (modulo  $25$ ), so there are no solutions in this case as  $b>0$ . $Case$   $2.3$ )   $a=4$ :  $24+5^{b}=7^{c}$ . Again, modulo  $3$  gives that  $b$  is even. Modulo  $25$  yields that  $c$  is even, so  $7^{2c_{1}}-5^{2b_{1}}=24$ . However,  $7^{c}-5^{b}\geq 7^{2c_{1}}-(7^{c_{1}}-2)^{2}=4\times (7^{c_{1}}-1)\geq 24$ . Equality occurs iff  $c_{1}=1$ , so we reach the solution  $(a,b,c)=(4,2,2)$ . $\boxed{\text{Answer: }(a,b,c)=(3,0,1), (2,1,1), (4,2,2)}$

stem_md: There is a non-equilateral triangle  $ABC$ .Let  $ABC$ 's Incentri  $I$ .Point  $D$  is on the  $BC$  side.The circle drawn outside the triangle  $IBD$  and  $ICD$  intersects the sides  $AB$  and  $AC$  at points  $E$  and  $F.$ The circle drawn outside the triangle  $DEF$  intersects the sides  $AB$  and  $AC$  at  $N$  and  $M$ .Prove that  $EM\parallel FN $ .
solution_md:
This problem is just a simple angle chasing. At first let's call  $\angle BAC = 2\theta, \angle CBA = 2\alpha, \angle BCA = 2\beta. => \angle DBI = \angle EBI = \alpha$  and  $\angle DCI = \angle ICF = \beta$ .
As we can see  $BDIE, DCFI, NFEM$  and  $EFDM$  are all cyclic =>  $\angle DBI = \angle EDI = \angle IED = \alpha, \angle DCI = \angle IFD = \angle IDF = \beta$ , but this implies that  $IE = ID = IF$ , i.e.,  $I$  is the circuncenter of  $\triangle DEF$  (not usefull at all), and  $\angle EDF = \angle EMF = \alpha + \beta$ . But  $NFME$  is cyclic, thus  $\angle ENF + \angle  EMF = 180^\circ$   $=>$   $\alpha + \beta + \angle ENF = 180^\circ$  =>  $\angle ENF = 2\theta + \alpha + \beta$  and  $\angle ANF = \alpha + \beta$ , thus  $\angle ANF = \angle AFN = \angle AME = \alpha + \beta$  if and only if  $EM \parallel FN $ .

stem_md:
Denote  $\mathbb{Z}_{>0}=\{1,2,3,...\}$  the set of all positive integers. Determine all functions  $f:\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$  such that, for each positive integer  $n$ , $\hspace{1cm}i) \sum_{k=1}^{n}f(k)$  is a perfect square, and $\vspace{0.1cm}$  $\hspace{1cm}ii) f(n)$  divides  $n^3$ .

*Proposed by Dorlir Ahmeti, Albania*
solution_md:
Nice and easy - posting for storage.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>$f(n) = n^3$  or all  $n \in \mathbb{N}$  is the only solution to the functional equation. This satisfies the two conditions as   $$ \sum_{k=1}^{n}f(k) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} k^3 = (\sum_{k=1}^{n} k)^2  $$</details>
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We shall prove that  $f(n) = n^3$  for each positive integer by strong induction on  $n$ .  $\textbf{Base Case:}$   $n=1$  
Notice that  $f(1) \mid 1^3=1$  meaning that  $1^3 = 1= f(1)$ .  $\textbf{Inductive Hypothesis:}$  
Assume that  $f(k)=k^3$  for all  $1 \leq k \leq n-1$ .  $\textbf{Inductive Step:}$  
Notice that   $$ \sum_{k=1}^{n} f(k) = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} k^3  + f(n) = (\frac{n(n-1)}{2})^2 + f(n+1)  $$  We know that the previous expression must be a perfect square meaning that   $$ f(n) = 2m(\frac{n(n-1)}{2})+m^2 = m(n(n-1)+m) $$   for some  $m \in \mathbb{N}$ . 
We therefore have that   $$ n(n-1)+m \mid f(n) \mid n^3 $$  Moreover,  $n(n-1)+m \mid n(n-1)(n+1)+m(n+1)$  meaning that   $$ n(n-1)+m \mid mn+m-n $$  Notice that for  $1 \leq m \leq n-1$  then  $n(n-1)+m > mn+m-n > 0$  which is a contradiction, also notice that if  $m=n$ , we have that  $f(n) = n^3$ , furthermore, if  $m > n$ , then  $f(n) > n^3$  which is not possible as  $f(n)$  must be a divisor of  $n^3$ . 
Ultimately, we must have that  $f(n)=n^3$  which completes our inductive step.  $\blacksquare$</details>

Note  $\left( \frac{k(k+1)}{2} \right)^2 + \frac{(k+1)^3}{b} = (k+1)^2 \left( \frac{k^2}{4} + \frac{k+1}{b}\right)$ . So  $k^2 +\frac{4k+4}{b}$  must be a rational square. Write  $k^2 +\frac{4k+4}{b} =\frac{p^2}{q^2}$  where  $p,q$  are coprime. Then  $q^2(bk^2+4k+4)=bp^2$ . Hence  $q^2 \mid b \implies b=lq^2 \implies l(qk)^2 + 4k+4 = lp^2$ . Hence  $b=1$  and thus  $f(k+1) = (k+1)^3$  completing our induction.

As  $f(n) \leq n^3$ :  $$ g(n)^2 \leq \sum_{k=1}^{n}{k^3}=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2 \Rightarrow g(n) \leq \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \quad \quad \left(\blacktriangle \right) $$  Also  $g$  is striclty increasing so  $g(n) \geq n$  for all  $n$ .

Now let  $n=p$  be prime. As  $f(p) \vert p^3$  we have  $f(p) \in \{1,p,p^2,p^3\}$ . As:  $$ f(p)=g(p)^2-g(p-1)^2=\left(g(p)-g(p-1)\right)\left(g(p)+g(p-1)\right) $$  and the second bracket is at least  $p+p-1>p$  we know  $f(p) \in \{p^2,p^3\}$ . Let  $k$  be a positive integer.  Determine the least positive integer  $n$ , with  $n\geq k+1$ , for which the game below can be played indefinitely:

Consider  $n$  boxes, labelled  $b_1,b_2,...,b_n$ . For each index  $i$ , box  $b_i$  contains exactly  $i$  coins. At each step, the following three substeps are performed in order:**(1)** Choose  $k+1$  boxes;**(2)** Of these  $k+1$  boxes, choose  $k$  and remove at least half of the coins from each, and add  to the remaining box, if labelled  $b_i$ , a number of  $i$  coins.**(3)** If one of the boxes is left empty, the game ends; otherwise, go to the next step.

*Proposed by Demetres Christofides, Cyprus*
solution_md: SolutionThe answer is $n = 2^k + k - 1$ . To show that this $n$ works, let $a_0 \leq a_1 \leq \cdots \leq a_k$ be the numbers of coins in the $k + 1$ largest-indexed boxes, in sorted order, and call a position *full* if $a_i \geq 2^i$ for each $0 \leq i \leq k$ . Then the initial position is full, and if we add to the box with $a_0$ coins (whose index is at least $2^k - 1$ ) and subtract from the other $k$ , fullness is preserved. Now we show that $n < 2^k + k - 1$ does not work. For any positive integer $n$ , let $f(n)$ be the greatest nonnegative integer $r$ with $2^r \leq n$ . If box $i$ has $c_i$ coins, let the *score* of the position be $\sum f(c_i)$ over all boxes $i$ . **Claim:** $f(x + y - 1) \leq f(x) + f(y)$ . *Proof.* If $x$ or $y$ is $1$ this is clearly true. Otherwise let $f(x) = r$ and $f(y) = s$ , with $r \geq s \geq 1$ . Then \[x + y - 1 < 2^{r + 1} + 2^{s + 1} - 1 < 2^{r + 1} + 2^{r + 1} = 2^{r + 2} \leq 2^{r + s + 1},\] which means $f(x + y - 1) \leq r + s$ . $\blacksquare$ If we remove at least half the coins from box $i$ , this subtracts at least $1$ from $f(c_i)$ . Meanwhile, if we add $i$ coins to box $i$ , by the above claim this adds at most $f(i + 1) \leq k$ coins to box $i$ , and equality holds for at most $k$ values of $i$ . So the score can never increase in a step, and there are at most $k$ boxes (chosen as the box being added to) for which the score remains the same. The score is always a nonnegative integer, so after some point we must *only* add to one of those $k$ boxes. But then we must subtract from one of the remaining $n - k$ boxes, which means the number of coins in those $n - k$ boxes strictly decreases every step, contradiction.

Step  $1$ . Halve boxes  $b_{2^k-1+i}$  where  $i \ne 0$  and add to box  $b_{2^k-1}$ .
Step  $2$ . Halve boxes  $b_{2^k-1+i}$  where  $i \ne 1$  and add to box  $b_{2^k}$ .  $$ \vdots $$  Step  $k+1$ .  Halve boxes  $b_{2^k-1+i}$  where  $i \ne k$  and add to box  $b_{2^k+k-1}$ .

The problem asks us to prove that for all large highly composite  $n$ , there is a highly composite number between  $n$  and  $\tfrac 32n$ .
---------------------
We will use a few well known facts about Highly Composite numbers. 

 

- If  $n=2^{e_1}\cdot 3^{e_2} \cdot \dots$  then  $e_1\geq e_2\geq \dots$
- For all primes  $p$  and a positive integer  $k$  there are only finitely many HC numbers  $n$  with  $\nu_p(n)<k$ .
**Claim :** For all primes  $p,q$  and a sufficiently large HC number  $n$  we have the identity :  $$  \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac {\nu_p(n)}{\nu_q(n)} = \frac { \log q }{ \log p } $$  *Proof :* Fix primes  $p$  and  $q$  and  $a,b \in \mathbb N$  such that  $p^a>q^b$ . Now there exists a  $N$  such that all HC numbers  $>N$ , say  $n$  is divisible by  $p^aq^b$ . (by the second fact) Let  $x= \nu_p (n)+1$  and  $y= \nu_q(n)+1$ . We get  $$  \tau(n) > \tau ( n\cdot \tfrac {q^b}{p^a}) \implies bx-ay < ab $$  This implies  $bx-ay$  is bounded above. In other words we have :  $$  \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac {\nu_p(n)}{\nu_q(n)}  \leq \frac ab $$  Take  $\tfrac ab$  to be arbitrarily close to  $\tfrac  { \log q }{ \log p }$  and this proves the upper bound. Similarly we can prove the lower bound. So the claim holds.
--------------------

Fix primes  $5$  and  $7$ . We will use the deep number-theoretic fact that  $\tfrac 75 > \tfrac 32$ . The claim implies that for all large enough HC  $n$  we have  $\nu_5(n)> \nu_7(n)+1$ . A short computation shows that  $\tau (\tfrac 75n)> \tau (n)$ , so we are done.  $\blacksquare$ .

Therefore, in the prime factorization of $\{a_n\}$ , the index of a smaller prime is always larger than the index of a larger prime. **Claim.** Let $C$ be a constant, for all sufficiently large $i$ we have $v_3(a_i)> C$ . stem_md: Let  $a_0>0$  be a real number, and let  $$ a_n=\frac{a_{n-1}}{\sqrt{1+2020\cdot a_{n-1}^2}}, \quad \textrm{for } n=1,2,\ldots ,2020. $$  Show that  $a_{2020}<\frac1{2020}$ .
solution_md: The problem can be restated as  $(\tfrac{1}{a_n})^2-(\tfrac{1}{a_{n-1}})^2=2020$ . So we get   $$ \frac{1}{a_{2020}^2} > \frac{1}{a_{2020}^2}-\frac{1}{a_0^2}=(2020)^2 $$   So  $\tfrac{1}{2020}>a_{2020}$  as desired.  $\square$

We want to prove by induction:
\[
0<a_n<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2020n}}
\]
for  $n\geq1$ .

Since  $a_0>0$ , we have  $a_1=\frac{a_0}{\sqrt{1+2020a_0^2}}>0$  and  $a_1=\frac{a_0}{\sqrt{1+2020a_0^2}}<\frac{a_0}{\sqrt{2020a_0^2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2020}}$ .

If  $0<a_n<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2020n}}$ , we have  $a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n}{\sqrt{1+2020a_n^2}}>0$  and
\[
a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n}{\sqrt{1+2020a_n^2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{a_n^2}+2020}}<\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2020n}}\right)^2}+2020}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2020(n+1)}}
\]

Thus  $a_{2020}<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2020\cdot2020}}=\frac{1}{2020}$ .

A much simpler solution:

Note that
\[
\frac{1}{a_n^2} = \frac{1}{a_{n-1}^2}+2020\implies \frac{1}{a_n^2}-\frac{1}{a_{n-1}^2} = 2020.
\]
Taking a telescoping sum, we thus obtain
\[
\frac{1}{a_n^2} = \frac{1}{a_1^2}+2020(n-1).
\]
Now,
\[
a_1 = \frac{a_0}{1+2020\cdot a_0^2}<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2020}}\implies \frac{1}{a_1^2}>2020.
\]
Hence, 
\[
\frac{1}{a_n^2}>2020n \implies a_n <\frac{1}{\sqrt{2020 n}}.
\]
Hence the result.

My solution during the contest:

There are  $x,y,z\in\mathbb{R}^+$  with  $a=\frac{x}{y},b=\frac{y}{z},c=\frac{z}{x}$ . We need to prove
\[
\sqrt{\frac{x^2}{y^2+z^2}}+\sqrt{\frac{y^2}{z^2+x^2}}+\sqrt{\frac{z^2}{x^2+y^2}}>2
\]
Define  $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in(0,1)$  by  $\alpha=\frac{x^2}{x^2+y^2+z^2},\beta=\frac{y^2}{x^2+y^2+z^2},\gamma=\frac{z^2}{x^2+y^2+z^2}$ . Note that  $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=1$ . We need to prove
\[
\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}}+\sqrt{\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}}+\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}}>2
\]
Since  $\alpha<1$  we have
\begin{align*}
\alpha(2\alpha-1)^2\geq0
\alpha\geq4\alpha^2(1-\alpha)
\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\geq4\alpha^2
\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}}\geq2\alpha
\end{align*}
Since  $\alpha>0$  equality holds if and only if  $\alpha=\frac{1}{2}$ . We have analogous inequalities for  $\beta,\gamma$ . Thus
\[
\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}}+\sqrt{\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}}+\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}}\geq2(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=2

stem_md:
Find all functions  $f:\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$  so that
\[f(f(x)+x+y) = f(x+y) + y f(y)\]
for all real numbers  $x, y$ .
solution_md:
We claim the only solution is  $\boxed{f(x)=0\quad\forall x}$  which works.

Suppose there exists  $a$  such that  $f(a) = b \ne 0.$  $P(a,0) \implies f(f(a) + a) = f(a) = b,$  then  $P(f(a) + a,a) \implies f(2b+2a) = f(b+2a) + ab$  and  $P(a,f(a) + a) \implies f(2b+2a) = f(b+2a) + (f(a) + a)b.$  Subtracting these two equations yields  $f(a)b = 0$  which is contradiction.  $\square$

We claim the only solution is  $\boxed{(0,0,0)}$ . Notice that since  $x$ ,  $y$ , and  $z$  are real, we must have that 
\begin{align*}
-4y(y^2z+z^2) &\ge 0 
x^4-4z^3 &\ge 0 
y^4-4x^2y &\ge 0
\end{align*}
due to the non-negativity of the discriminant. Now, adding them all gives that \[-4y(y^2z+z^2)+x^4-4z^3+y^4-4x^2y \ge 0\] implying that \[x^4+y^4 \ge 4y(y^2z+z^2)+4x^2y+4z^3\] which means that \[\dfrac{1}{4}(x^4+y^4) \ge y^3z+yz^2+x^2y+z^3.\] However, equality is only attained when  $x = y = z = 0$  after solving the equation given by the discriminant, so we are done.  $\square$

Rearranging, we find the equivalent

If  $y=0$ , this shows that  $z=0$  and hence  $x=0$  which is a solution. If  $z=0$ , we also get  $y=0$ .
From now on assume that  $y,z  \ne 0$ . Hence
\[4(y-1)z(y^2+z) \ge y^4>0.\]
On the other hand, remember from the first equation that
\[yz(z+y^2)=-x^2y^2  <  0.\]
Hence  $y$  and  $y-1$  must have different signs and hence  $y \in (0,1)$  so that  $z<0$  and  $y^2+z>0$ . But now AM-GM implies that
\[4(y-1)z(y^2+z)=(1-y) \cdot 4\vert z\vert \cdot (y^2-\vert z\vert) \le (1-y)y^4<y^4\]
which is a contradiction.

<details><summary>Motivation</summary>It should be very natural to eliminate one equation and one variable. This leads to the equation in two variables  $y,z$ . At this point, for each fixed  $z$ , we except solutions for  $y$ , unless something special happens.
Since we don't find a parameter family of solutions (like  $y=z^2$  always works), we expect that "something special" should happen which means that some inequality must prevent us from having real solutions (since complex solutions will always be there).
But in fact it is easily verified that the equation in  $y,z$  has non-trivial (and very ugly!) real solutions.
So where is our mistake? We forgot that  $x$  also has to be real. From this we get an inequality on  $y,z$  from the first equation and combining the two in a clever way it is then not too hard to find something like the above solution.</details>

stem_md: Let  $n>2$  be a given positive integer. There are  $n$  guests at Georg's bachelor party and each guest is friends with at least one other guest. Georg organizes a party game among the guests. Each guest receives a jug of water such that there are no two guests with the same amount of water in their jugs. All guests now proceed simultaneously as follows. Every guest takes one cup for each of his friends at the party and distributes all the water from his jug evenly in the cups. He then passes a cup to each of his friends. Each guest having received a cup of water from each of his friends pours the water he has received into his jug. What is the smallest possible number of guests that do not have the same amount of water as they started with?
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2020 Contests/2020 Baltic Way/2342208.json

candidates: Answer deleted

As mentioned above, the answer is 2.

Construction:
Arrange the guests in a row, and let two people be friends iff they are next to each other.
n even: Let the guests have 0, 1, 2, ..., n-3, n-2, (n-1)/2 litres of water respectively (note that the last value is not an integer, so it doesn't overlap with any of the previous ones)
n odd: Let the guests have 0.5, 2, 3, ..., n-2, n-1, n/2 litres of water respectively (again, n/2 is not an integer).

Bound:
We shall show that there is a guest who ends up with less water than they started with. Suppose otherwise.
Consider the value (starting amount of water)/(number of friends) for each guest; pick any guest who maximises this; let his (starting amount of water)/(number of friends) be M. Then he receives at most M litres of water from each friend, and so his amount of water does not increase. For equality to hold, all his friends must also have (starting amount of water)/(number of friends) equal to M. Repeating this argument for each of them, we get that everyone in this connected component in the friendship graph has (starting amount of water)/(number of friends) equal to M. Applying Euler's Handshaking Lemma on this connected component, two people have the same number of friends, and so the same starting amount of water, contradiction.
Since the total amount of water is invariant, someone also ends up with more water than they started with.
Hence, at least 2 people don't end up with the same amount of water they started with.

stem_md:
A mason has bricks with dimensions  $2\times5\times8$  and other bricks with dimensions  $2\times3\times7$ . She also has a box with dimensions  $10\times11\times14$ . The bricks and the box are all rectangular parallelepipeds. The mason wants to pack bricks into the box filling its entire volume and with no bricks sticking out.
Find all possible values of the total number of bricks that she can pack.
solution_md:
Denote: $\bullet\;$  brick of type A: with dimensions  $2\times5\times8$ ; $\bullet\;$  brick of type B: with dimensions  $2\times3\times7$ .
The box contains  $10\cdot11\cdot14=1540$  unit cubes; a brick of type A contains  $2\cdot5\cdot8=80$  unit cubes; a brick of type B contains  $2\cdot3\cdot7=42$  unit cubes.

The possible number of bricks is a non-negative integer solution of the equation: $80x+42y=1540\Longrightarrow 21y=10(77-4x)\Longrightarrow y=10m$ , where  $m\in\mathbb{Z}\Longrightarrow$  $\Longrightarrow 21m=77-4x\Longrightarrow x=\dfrac{77-21m}{4}=19-5m-\dfrac{m-1}{4}\in\mathbb{Z}\Longrightarrow$  $\Longrightarrow \dfrac{m-1}{4}=n\in\mathbb{Z}\Longrightarrow m=4n+1$ .
Results: $x=14-21n\;;y=40n+10$ . $x\ge0\;;y\ge0\Longrightarrow n=0\Longrightarrow x=14\;;y=10$ .
Hence, the equation has an unique non-negative integer solution:  $(x,y)=(14,10)$  and  $x+y=24$ .

Remains to prove: we can fill the box with a configuration of  $14$  bricks A and  $10$  bricks B.
The solution in plane: we can fill a  $7\times11$  rectangle with: a rectangle  $2\times8$ , a rectangle  $5\times8$  and a rectangle  $3\times7$ . Results: we can fill a  $11\times14$  rectangle with:  $2$  rectangles  $2\times8$ ,  $2$  rectangles  $5\times8$  and  $2$  rectangles  $3\times7$ .
The solution in space: 
The base of the box is the rectangle  $11\times14$  and the height is  $10$ .
We can put in the box:  $2$  columns, each containing  $2$  bricks A with the base  $2\times8$  and the height  $5$ ; $2$  columns, each containing  $5$  bricks A with the base  $5\times8$  and the height  $2$ ; $2$  columns, each containing  $5$  bricks B with the base  $3\times7$  and the height  $2$ .

Final answer: the total number of bricks is  $24$ , respectively  $14$  bricks with the dimensions  $2\times5\times8$  and  $10$  bricks with the dimensions  $2\times3\times7$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2020 Contests/2020 Baltic Way/2342211.json

stem_md:
Let  $n$  be a given positive integer. 
A restaurant offers a choice of  $n$  starters,  $n$  main dishes,  $n$  desserts and  $n$  wines. 
A merry company dines at the restaurant, with each guest choosing a starter, a main dish, a dessert and a wine.  
No two people place exactly the same order. 
It turns out that there is no collection of  $n$  guests such that their orders coincide in three of these aspects, 
but in the fourth one they all differ. (For example, there are no  $n$  people that order exactly the same three courses of food, but  $n$  different wines.) What is the maximal number of guests?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>For  $n=1$ , the answer is clearly  $1$ . From now on assume that  $n \ge 2$ .
For each triple of (starter, main dish, dessert), only  $n-1$  of the wines can be ordered.
So there can be at most  $n^3(n-1)$  different orders.
On the other hand, we can find a set of  $n^3(n-1)$  orders satisfying the conditions by numbering the possibilities in each category from  $1,2,\dots,n$  and choosing all orders where the sum of the four numbers is not divisible by  $n$ .

So the answer is  $1$  for  $n=1$  and  $n^4-n^3$  for  $n \ge 2$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2020 Contests/2020 Baltic Way/2342212.json

stem_md: Alice and Bob are playing hide and seek. Initially, Bob chooses a secret fixed point  $B$  in the unit square. Then Alice chooses a sequence of points  $P_0, P_1, \ldots, P_N$  in the plane. After choosing  $P_k$  (but before choosing  $P_{k+1}$ ) for  $k \geq 1$ , Bob tells "warmer'' if  $P_k$  is closer to  $B$  than  $P_{k-1}$ , otherwise he says "colder''. After Alice has chosen  $P_N$  and heard Bob's answer, Alice chooses a final point  $A$ . Alice wins if the distance  $AB$  is at most  $\frac 1 {2020}$ , otherwise Bob wins. Show that if  $N=18$ , Alice cannot guarantee a win.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Effectively, what Alice can do is to choose  $18$  lines and she will find out on which side of this line, the point  $B$  happens to be (with the case of  $B$  being on that line belonging to one specific side of that line). One can now argue in two different ways that she cannot win too quickly:
<details><summary>Via area</summary>In the worst case, the point  $B$  is always in the remaining part which has the larger area. So no matter which  $18$  lines she chooses, it can happen that the remaining possible part has area at least  $\frac{1}{2^{18}}$ .
But supposing she can win, she would have to know that  $B$  is in a certain disc with radius  $\frac{1}{2020}$ .
But this disc has area  $\frac{\pi}{2020^2}<\frac{4}{1024^2}=\frac{1}{2^{18}}$ .</details>
<details><summary>Via lattice points</summary>Consider the  $(N+1)^2$  points with coordinates multiples of  $\frac{1}{N}$  inside the unit square. In the worst case, the point  $B$  is always in the remaining part which has the larger number of these points. So no matter which  $18$  lines she chooses, it can happen that the remaining possible part has at least  $\frac{(N+1)^2}{2^{18}}$  points in it.
If  $N=2^9$ , this is more than one, so it can happen that there are two points in this part with distance at least  $\frac{1}{N}=\frac{1}{512}$ .
So she cannot do better than half the distance of these points, i.e. not better than  $\frac{1}{1024}>\frac{1}{2020}$ .</details></details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2020 Contests/2020 Baltic Way/2342216.json

stem_md: Let  $ABC$  be a triangle with  $AB > AC$ . The internal angle bisector of  $\angle BAC$  intersects the side  $BC$  at  $D$ . The circles with diameters  $BD$  and  $CD$  intersect the circumcircle of  $\triangle ABC$  a second time at  $P \not= B$  and  $Q \not= C$ , respectively. The lines  $PQ$  and  $BC$  intersect at  $X$ . Prove that  $AX$  is tangent to the circumcircle of  $\triangle ABC$ .
solution_md:
Let  $PD$  and  $QD$  intersect  $(ABC)$  again at  $B'$  and  $C'$ , respectively, and let  $M$  be the midpoint of arc  $BC$  not containing  $A$ . Also let  $D'$  be the reflection of  $D$  over the midpoint of  $BC$ . Clearly  $B'$  and  $C'$  are the antipodes of  $B$  and  $C$  and  $M$  lies on  $AD$ .

Now negative inversion at  $D$  fixing  $(ABC)$  swaps  $(B,C),(P,B'),(Q,C'),(A,M)$  and thus maps  $BC\to BC$ ,  $PQ\to (B'DD'C')$  and  $AA\to (DMD')$ . Since these all intersect at  $D'$ , inverting back we get that  $BC$ ,  $PQ$  and  $AA$  are concurrent.

stem_md:
On a plane, Bob chooses 3 points  $A_0$ ,  $B_0$ ,  $C_0$  (not necessarily distinct) such that  $A_0B_0+B_0C_0+C_0A_0=1$ . Then he chooses points  $A_1$ ,  $B_1$ ,  $C_1$  (not necessarily distinct) in such a way that  $A_1B_1=A_0B_0$  and  $B_1C_1=B_0C_0$ .
Next he chooses points  $A_2$ ,  $B_2$ ,  $C_2$  as a permutation of points  $A_1$ ,  $B_1$ ,  $C_1$ . Finally, Bob chooses points  $A_3$ ,  $B_3$ ,  $C_3$  (not necessarily distinct) in such a way that  $A_3B_3=A_2B_2$  and  $B_3C_3=B_2C_2$ . What are the smallest and the greatest possible values of  $A_3B_3+B_3C_3+C_3A_3$  Bob can obtain?
solution_md:
My solution during the contest:

We have:
\begin{align*}
A_3B_3+B_3C_3+C_3A_3\leq2(A_3B_3+B_3C_3)=2(A_2B_2+B_2C_2)
\leq2(A_1B_1+B_1C_1+C_1A_1-\min\{A_1B_1,B_1C_1,C_1A_1\})
\leq2(2A_1B_1+2B_1C_1-\min\{A_1B_1,B_1C_1\})=2(2A_0B_0+2B_0C_0-\min\{A_0B_0,B_0C_0\})
=3(A_0B_0+B_0C_0)+(A_0B_0+B_0C_0-2\min\{A_0B_0,B_0C_0\})
\leq3(A_0B_0+B_0C_0)+C_0A_0\leq3(A_0B_0+B_0C_0+C_0A_0)=3
\end{align*}
Equality can be reached if  $A_0=C_0$ , the points  $A_1=C_2,B_1=A_2,C_1=B_2$  are in this order on a straight line and the points  $A_3,B_3,C_3$  are in this order on a straight line. Thus the maximum is  $3$ .

Switching  $A_0,B_0,C_0,A_1,B_1,C_1$  with  $A_3,B_3,C_3,A_2,B_2,C_2$ , we get that the minimum is  $\frac{1}{3}$ .

stem_md:
Richard and Kaarel are taking turns to choose numbers from the set  $\{1,\dots,p-1\}$  where  $p > 3$  is a prime. Richard is the first one to choose. A number which has been chosen by one of the players cannot be chosen again by either of the players. Every number chosen by Richard is multiplied with the next number chosen by Kaarel.

Kaarel wins the game if at any moment after his turn the sum of all of the products calculated so far is divisible by  $p$ . Richard wins if this does not happen, i.e. the players run out of numbers before any of the sums is divisible by  $p$ . Can either of the players guarantee their victory regardless of their opponent's moves and if so, which one?
solution_md:
Kaarel wins.

Suppose Richard chooses  $a$  in the beginning. Kaarel then chooses  $p-a$ . Next, Richard chooses  $b$ . If Kaarel's number,  $c$ , satisfies:
\[
a(p-a)+bc\equiv 0\pmod{p}\Leftrightarrow c\equiv \frac{a^2}{b}\pmod{p},
\]
Kaarel wins. Let us now ensure that  $c\triangleq \frac{a^2}{b}$  is not chosen before. Since  $a\not\equiv b\pmod{p}$ ,  $c$  is distinct from  $a$ . Likewise, if  $c\equiv -a\pmod{p}$ , then  $b\equiv-a\pmod{p}$ , but  $p-a$  is already chosen by Kaarel. Finally, if  $c\equiv b\pmod{p}$ , then  $a\equiv \pm b\pmod{p}$ . But both  $a$  as well as  $p-a$  are chosen in the beginning respectively by Richard and Kaarel. Hence, Richard cannot choose one of these in round 2 as his  $b$ . Hence the conclusion.

stem_md: For a prime number  $p$  and a positive integer  $n$ , denote by  $f(p, n)$  the largest integer  $k$  such that  $p^k \mid n!$ . Let  $p$  be a given prime number and let  $m$  and  $c$  be given positive integers. Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers  $n$  such that  $f(p, n) \equiv c \pmod m$ .
solution_md:
We use the base- $p$  digit sum version of Legendre's formula:\[v_p(n!) = \frac{n - S_p(n)}{p - 1}\]
where  $S_p(n)$  denotes the sum of the digits of  $n$  in base  $p$ .
We want to prove that for any given prime  $p$  and positive integers  $m$  and  $c$ , there exist infinitely many positive integers  $n$  such that
\[v_p(n!) \equiv c \pmod{m}.\] Assume\[v_p(n!) = mk + c \quad \text{for } k = 1, 2, 3, \dots\]
Then, by the formula:\[\frac{n - S_p(n)}{p - 1} = mk + c \Rightarrow n - S_p(n) = (p - 1)(mk + c)\]
Now we try to construct such  $n$ . Let  $n = y \cdot p^x$  for some integer  $y$  and exponent  $x \geq 1$ .
Then, since multiplying  $y$  by  $p^x$  simply adds zeros to its base- $p$  representation,\[S_p(n) = S_p(y),\]
so\[n - S_p(n) = y \cdot p^x - S_p(y).\]
Suppose we choose  $y$  such that  $S_p(y) = y$  (i.e.,  $y$  is a single digit in base  $p$ ), then:\[n - S_p(n) = y(p^x - 1).\]
Thus, we want:\[y(p^x - 1) = (p - 1)(mk + c).\]

solution_md:
If you don't see the tricky factorization above (like myself), you can do the following long but more technical round for  $f(101)$ .

We claim that for every  $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{101}$ , there is a triple  $(x,y,z)$  such that  $101\mid x^2+y^2+z^2$  and  $xyz\equiv k\pmod{101}$ . For  $k=0$ , this is immediate by taking  $x=y=z=0$ , hence suppose  $k\ne 0$  in the remainder. 

Our goal is to show, for every  $1\le k\le 100$ , there exists a  $1\le a\le 100$  such that for some  $y,z$  the following holds:
\[
y^2+z^2\equiv -a^2\pmod{101}\quad\text{and}\quad yz\equiv \frac{k}{a}\pmod{101}.
\]
Now, since  $101\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ ,  $-1$  is a quadratic residue, modulo  $101$ . Let  $u\in\mathbb{Z}_{101}$  be such that  $u^2\equiv -1\pmod{101}$ , and let  $y\equiv t_y\cdot u\cdot a\pmod{101}$  and  $z\equiv t_z\cdot u\cdot a\pmod{101}$ . Note that if such a  $t_y,t_z$  can be found, one can also find  $y,z$  and conclude the case. Now, in terms of these objects, it suffices to show there exists  $a$  such that the following holds for some  $t_y,t_z$ :
\[
t_y^2+t_z^2\equiv 1\pmod{101}\quad\text{and}\quad t_yt_z\equiv -\frac{k}{a^3}\pmod{101}.
\]
Since  $101\equiv 2\pmod{3}$ , it follows  $a\mapsto -\frac{1}{a^3}\pmod{101}$  is injective, except  $a\ne 0$ . Hence, it suffices to show, there exists an  $a'$  for which for some  $t_y,t_z$  it holds:
\[
t_y^2+t_z^2\equiv 1\pmod{101}\quad\text{and}\quad t_yt_z\equiv a'k\pmod{101}.
\]
Observing  $t_y^2+t_z^2+2t_yt_z=\left(t_y+t_z\right)^2$  and  $t_y^2+t_z^2-2t_yt_z=\left(t_y-t_z\right)^2$ , it suffices to show for some  $a'$ , the objects
\[
1+2a'k \quad\text{and}\quad 1-2a'k
\]
are both quadratic residues, modulo  $p$ . Now, we observe that both  $6$  and  $-4$  are quadratic residues, modulo  $101$ . Hence, setting  $2a'k\equiv 5\pmod{101}$  works. Namely, for any {\bf fixed}  $k$ , taking
\[
a'\equiv \frac{5}{2k}\pmod{101}
\]
works. Hence, the claim is complete, and that,  $f(101)=101$ .**Remark.** I am fairly confident that a reverse engineering of what I did above gives (something very similar to) the slick solution above.

This problem was proposed by **[Burii](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/user/100466)**.

Let  $A = \{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n \}$  and  $B = \{b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_m \}$ . Notice that if  $S$  contains three elements of the form  $(a_i \cdot x)$ ,  $(y \cdot b_j)$  and  $(a_i \cdot b_j)$ , then  $ a_ib_j \mid (a_i \cdot x) \cdot (y \cdot b_j) $  and problem would be done. Let's prove  $S$  always contains  $3$  such elements. 

Elements of  $S$  are always in the form  $a_i \cdot b_j$ , thus  $S$  can be represented by the edges of a bipartite graph, where  $a_ib_j$  is represented by the edge  $a_i - b_j$ . If this graph contains chain of  $3$  edges say  $a_i - b_j$ ,  $b_j - a_k$  and  $a_k - b_e$ , the problem is solved since  $b_j a_k \mid a_kb_e \cdot a_ib_j $ . Assume graph does not contain such chain. This graph must not contain any cycles, because cycle would have to be of length at least  $4$  and in it would be chain of length  $3$ , which is impossible.
Then this graph consists of multiple trees. The number of trees can be calculated by the well- known formula ((number of vertices) -(number of edges )). But this graph has  $n+m$  vertices and  $n+m-1$  edges, so in fact this graph is connected tree.  A tree of more than  $4$  vertices must have a chain of 3 edges, otherwise it is a *star*type tree, but degree of each edge is limited by  $\max(n,m)$ , so our graph cannot be *star.*. This ends proof.

Define $O$ to be the center of $\omega$ . **Claim.** $OKAB$ is cyclic. *Proof.* Note that $\angle O_BMB = 90^{\circ} - \angle BAM$ . So, $\angle KOM = 180 - 2 \cdot \angle O_BMB = 2 \cdot \angle BAM$ . But, \begin{align*} \angle KAB = 180 - \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot \angle KOM - \angle BAM = 180 - 2 \cdot \angle BAM. \end{align*} Therefore, $\angle KOB + \angle KAB = 180^{\circ}$ and $OKAB$ is cyclic, as desired. $\blacksquare$ So, $\angle AMK = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot \angle AOK = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot \angle ABK$ . Then, \begin{align*} \angle KBM &= \angle ABK + \angle ABM &= 2 \cdot \angle AMK + \angle O_CO_BM &= \left(180 - \angle AO_BM\right) + \angle O_CO_BM &= 180 - \angle AO_BO_C = 180 - \angle O_CO_BM = \angle OO_BM. \end{align*} Thus, $\triangle OO_BM \sim \triangle KBM$ . Then, $\angle AKM \cong \angle O_BOM \cong \angle O_BKB$ . Thus, $KB$ intersects $\omega$ at the reflection of $A$ across $BC$ , at say $D$ . Now, we want to show $C$ , $D$ , and $L$ are collinear. Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $M$ be any point on segment $BC$ . Denote by $O_B$ and $O_C$ the circumcenters of $\triangle ABM$ and $\triangle ACM$ , respectively. Suppose $\omega$ is a circle whose center lies on $\overline{BC}$ and passes through $A$ and $M$ . Lines $MO_B$ and $MO_C$ meet $\omega$ again at $K$ and $L$ , respectively. Prove that lines $BK$ and $CL$ meet on $\omega$ .
Let $A'$ denote the reflection of $A$ over $\overline{BC}.$ I claim that lines $BL$ and $CL$ meet at $A'$ (which obviously lies on $\omega$ ). It suffices to show that $A', B,$ and $K$ are collinear because then it will follow by symmetry that $A', C,$ and $L$ are collinear as well. Let $H_B$ denote the orthocenter of $\triangle{ABM}.$ Then, we have \begin{align*} A', B, K \text{ collinear} &\iff \angle{ABK}+\angle{ABA'}=180^\circ &\iff \angle{ABK}+2\angle{ABC}=180^\circ &\iff \angle{ABK} = 180^\circ-2\angle{ABC} &\iff \angle{ABK}=180^\circ-\angle{AO_BM} &\iff \angle{ABK}=\angle{AO_BK} &\iff AO_BBK \text{ cyclic}. \end{align*} Then, since it is well-known $O_B$ and $H_B$ are isogonal conjugates, we know that \begin{align*} \angle{O_BKB} &= \angle{MKA'} &= \angle{MAA'} &= \angle{MAO_B}+\angle{O_BAH_B} &= \angle{BAH_B}+\angle{O_BAH_B} &= \angle{BAO_B}, \end{align*} we know that $AO_BBK$ is cyclic, so we are done. $\square$

Since  $BX = BA$  so  $\angle BXA = \angle BAX = 90^\circ - B$  and since  $K'BM = 90^\circ$  so  $\angle K'MA = \angle K'BA = 90^\circ - B = \angle AMK = \angle AXK$ , so  $K, B, X$  are collinear.  

Similarly,  $\angle AXL = \angle AML = 180^\circ - \angle AML' = 180^\circ - \angle ACL' = 180^\circ - (90^\circ - C) = 90^\circ + C$  and  $\angle AXC = \angle XAC = 90^\circ - C$ , so  $C, X, L$  are also collinear.

stem_md: Let  $S$  be a set of  $a+b+3$  points on a sphere, where  $a$ ,  $b$  are nonnegative integers and no four points of  $S$  are coplanar. Determine how many planes pass through three points of  $S$  and separate the remaining points into  $a$  points on one side of the plane and  $b$  points on the other side.
solution_md:
For the purposes of the proof, suppose  $\mathbb{N}$  includes  $0$ . 

The answer is  $2(a+1)(b+1)$  if  $a \neq b$  and  $(a+1)(b+1)$  if  $a = b.$ Say that a set of points in the plane is in **general position** if no three are collinear and no four are acyclic.

First, select an arbitrary point  $P$  on the sphere which does not lie on a plane passing through three of the points of  $S.$  

Consider applying an inversion about  $P$  of arbitrary radius. Clearly, there is now a plane  $\Pi$  containing the points of  $S$ . The condition of the problem implies that the points of  $S$  are in general position on  $\Pi.$ Note that a plane which, before the inversion, separated the points into  $a$  points on one side and  $b$  on the other is now a sphere through  $P$  which contains  $a$  (resp.  $b$ ) points and doesn't contain  $b$  (resp.  $a$ ) points (with  $3$  on its boundary). We just need to enumerate the number of such spheres in the inverted diagram. 

Since all points of  $S$  lie on the plane, it suffices to consider the cross sections of the spheres with the plane. This means that we only need to enumerate the number of circles passing through three points of  $S$  (on  $\Pi$ ) which contain precisely  $a$  points or precisely  $b$  points.

Hence, we simply need to show the following problem now:**Problem.** Given  $a+b+3$  points in the plane in general position, the number of circles which pass through  $3$  of the points and contain either exactly  $a$  or exactly  $b$  of the points in their strict interior is  $2(a+1)(b+1)$  if  $a \neq b$  and  $(a+1)(b+1)$  if  $a = b.$ So let's solve this problem. For a set  $S$  of  $n$  points in general position in the plane, let  $g_{S}(a, b)$  be the quantity described in the problem (which we want to prove is  $2(a+1)(b+1)$  if  $a \neq b$  and  $(a+1)(b+1)$  otherwise). 

For two integers  $a \le n-3 \in \mathbb{N}$ , we define the following. For a set  $S$  of  $n$  points in general position in the plane, let  $f_{S}(a)$  denote the number of circles which pass through three points of  $S$  and contain precisely  $a$  points in their boundary. **Claim.** For any  $a \le n-3 \in \mathbb{N}$  the following holds. Over all sets of  $n$  points in general position which comprise the vertices of a convex  $n-$ gon,  $f_{S}(a)$  is fixed.**Proof.** We will use dark magic. Let's show first that for two convex sets  $S_1, S_2$  of  $n$  points in general position which have  $n-1$  points in common,  $f_{S_1} (a) = f_{S_2} (a).$ Let  $P$  be the point in  $S_1$  which isn't in  $S_2$ , and let  $Q$  be the point in  $S_2$  which isn't in  $S_1.$  Consider a path from  $P$  to  $Q$  (not necessarily a straight line) so that as point  $P$  moves along this path (with  $S_1$  changing accordingly), at no point is there more than one cyclic quadrilateral in  $S_1$  and at no point are there three points of  $S_1$  collinear. It's easy to see that this path exists (just draw some pictures and note that there's only  $\binom{n-1}{3}$  circles we may have to cross). 

Now let's see what happens as  $P$  moves along this path. When  $P$  does not cross a circle, it's obvious that  $f_{S_1}(a)$  doesn't change. Suppose now that  $P$  crosses a circle. More specifically, suppose that  $A, B, C \in S_1 / \{P\}$  are such that  $P$  was formerly outside  $(\triangle ABC)$  but is now inside it.

We will show that the number of circles through three points of  $S_1$  which contain exactly  $a$  points in their interior is unchanged.

WLOG let quadrilateral  $BACP$  be convex. 

If  $(\triangle ABC)$  used to have exactly  $a$  points, then so did  $(\triangle PBC)$ . After the crossing,  $(\triangle ABP)$  and  $(\triangle ACP)$  have exactly  $a$  points. If  $(\triangle ABP)$  used to have exactly  $a$  points, then so did  $(\triangle ACP).$  After the crossing,  $(\triangle ABC)$  and  $(\triangle BCP)$  have exactly  $a$  points.

For all other circles (i.e. not among  $(\triangle ABC), (\triangle ABP), (\triangle ACP), (\triangle BCP)$ ), the number of points in their interior is unchanged.

So we've shown that the number of circles passing through three points of  $S_1$  with precisely  $a$  points in their interior is unchanging as we move  $P$  along this path.

Hence,  $f_{S_1} (a) = f_{S_2} (a)$  for all  $a \le n-3.$ It's also clear that we can transform any two convex sets into each other by making small adjustments to one point at a time, maintaining convexity. This means that, together with the above work, the claim is proven. $\blacksquare$ **Lemma 1.** Over all sets  $S$  with  $a+b+3$  points in general position,  $g_{S}(a, b)$  is constant.**Proof.** The proof of this is essentially the same as that of the claim. The exception is that points are now allowed to cross lines. The details are essentially the same. $\blacksquare$ From here, the rest is selecting a favorable configuration and computation. 

Observe that for any convex set  $S$  of  $a+b+3$  points for  $a, b \in \mathbb{N},$   $g_{S}(a, b) = f_{S}(a+b+3, a) + f_{S} (a+b+3, b)$  if  $a \neq b$  and  $g_{S}(a, b) = f_{S}(a+b+3, a)$  if  $a = b.$  The following lemma essentially finishes the problem off.

Let  $f(n, a)$  be the number which satisfies the following. For any set of  $n$  points in the plane which are in general position and form the vertices of a convex  $n-$ gon, there are precisely  $f(n, a)$  circles passing through three of the  $n$  points and containing  $a$  of the  $n$  points in their interior. This function is defined by the Claim.**Lemma 2.**  $f(a+b+3, b) = (a+1)(b+1)$  for all  $a, b \in \mathbb{N}.$  **Proof.** We will prove this by induction on  $b.$  When  $b = 0$ , let  $T$  be an arbitrary point in the plane. Let  $T_1, T_2, \cdots, T_{a+2}$  be  $a+2$  other points which are almost collinear. Suppose that when  $T$  views the  $T_i$ 's in clockwise order, it sees them in the order  $T_1, T_2, \cdots, T_{a+2}$  and  $\angle T_1TT_{A+2} < \frac{\pi}{1000}$ . Suppose that  $T$  is sufficiently far away from the  $T_i$ 's so that  $(\triangle TT_i T_{i+1})$  has none of the other  $T_j$ 's for  $1 \le i \le a+1$ , but it's also close enough that  $(\triangle T_i T_j T_k)$  contains  $T$  for any  $1 \le i < j < k \le a+2.$   This implies that  $f(a+3, 0) = a+1$ , which solves the base case.

Suppose it holds for  $b = k$ . When  $b = k+1$ , we do a similar thing as before. Again, select an arbitrary point  $T$  in the plane, and let  $T_1, T_2, \cdots, T_{a+k+3}$  be almost collinear so that  $T$  views them in exactly this clockwise order and  $\angle T_1 T T_{a+k+3} < \frac{\pi}{1000}.$  

Again suppose that  $T$  is sufficiently far so that  $(\triangle TT_i T_j)$  contains in its interior precisely the  $T_\ell$ 's with  $i < \ell < j$  for  $1 \le i < j \le a+k+3,$  but also close enough that  $(\triangle T_i T_j T_\ell)$  contains  $T$  for all  $1 \le i < j < \ell \le a+k+3.$  

It is then evident that  $f(a+k+4, k+1) = f(a+k+3, k) + a+1$ , because there are  $a+1$  circles which are of the form  $(\triangle T T_i T_{i+a+2})$  and  $f(a+k+3, k)$  circles which are of the form  $(\triangle T_i T_j T_\ell)$  which contain  $k$  of the  $T_h$ 's (in addition to containing  $T$ ).

From the induction hypothesis, we then obtain  $f(a+k+4, k+1) = (a+1)(k+1) + (a+1) = (a+1)(k+2)$ , completing the induction. $\blacksquare$ From the lemma, the result of the problem follows. $\square$
